slides.title: Four days of evidence, then one adoption decision you defend
slides.text: The course at a glance Four days of evidence, then one adoption decision you defend Day 1 · Tables A tuned baseline, a pretrained tabular model, learning curves, a leaderboard claim. Day 2 · Series Zero-shot forecasts on 400 series, by group, with Ramadan and Eid, and stacking. Day 3 · Decisions Quantiles into orders and trucks; forecasters ranked by the regret they cause. Day 4 · Shift and adoption A new region: shift found, validated, corrected; licence, cost and residency. Day 5 · Capstone. An evaluation protocol and an adoption decision for one task, in a public repository, defended before two assessors.

slides.title: Every new model meets a fair baseline, the same splits and an interval
slides.text: How this course works Every new model meets a fair baseline, the same splits and an interval Fair Same data, same folds, same metric, and the tuning budget written down. Sized A difference without an interval is an anecdote. Decided Accuracy is one column. Cost, licence and the data's classification are the others. AI policy. AI off for the supervised checks and for the Day 1 baseline (Lab 1.1). In the other labs an assistant may give hints, not finished pipelines. In the capstone, anything goes, with a verification note and a live defence.

slides.title: Bustan Food Wholesale wants to know which new models earn their place
slides.text: One case study all week Bustan Food Wholesale wants to know which new models earn their place A fictional food wholesaler with depots in Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Buraidah, and a new northern region around Hail and Tabuk. 80,000 orders Over three Hijri years, with delivery hours and a late flag. 8,000 of them come from the new region. 400 demand series 100 products at four depots, daily, with Ramadan and both Eids from the Umm al-Qura calendar. Costs and capacity Margins, holding and spoilage, trucks, reefers and depot space.

slides.title: Tuned boosted trees first
slides.text: Session 1 Tuned boosted trees first State a tuning budget in fits and seconds before comparing models Tune a boosted-tree model by random search under grouped cross-validation Explain why random K-fold flatters a model when customers repeat 01

slides.title: "Is the new model better?" means better than what, tuned how much?
slides.text: What Ahlam asks "Is the new model better?" means better than what, tuned how much? AhlamA vendor says its pretrained model predicts late deliveries better than anything we have. Should we switch? SarabBetter than our boosted trees after we tune them with the same effort, on our own customers. Give me today. The target Late: delivered after the promised hours. 18% of orders in the established regions. The trap An untuned baseline makes any new model look good.

slides.title: Write the tuning budget down before you search
slides.text: Before any search Write the tuning budget down before you search Budget item Lab 1.1 Why it is fixed first Configurations 20, drawn at random More draws always find a luckier one Folds 5, grouped by customer The estimate the search optimises Fits 100, plus 3 refits The unit a pretrained model is compared in Seconds measured, on a laptop CPU The cost the adoption memo reports A budget is part of the result. "AUC 0.78 after 103 fits" can be compared; "AUC 0.78" cannot.

slides.title: Six parameters, each with a range that a practitioner would defend
slides.text: What the search draws from Six parameters, each with a range that a practitioner would defend {"learning_rate": log-uniform 0.02 to 0.2, "num_leaves": 7, 15, 31 or 63, "min_child_samples": 10, 20, 50 or 100, "n_estimators": 100, 200 or 400, "colsample_bytree": 0.6, 0.8 or 1.0, "reg_lambda": 0, 1 or 5} The best of 20 in the course run: 7 leaves, learning rate 0.021, 400 trees, 60% of features per tree. Small trees and many of them.

slides.title: A customer seen in training is recognised, not predicted
slides.text: Why the folds must be grouped A customer seen in training is recognised, not predicted A customer's distance and segment never change: together they fingerprint the customer. Some customers are late more often for reasons in no column: their street, their receiving hours. Random folds put the same customer on both sides; the model learns the fingerprint. Bustan predicts for new and changing customers, so the folds keep each customer on one side. In the sample 5,000 orders from fewer than 1,500 customers: most customers appear more than once.

slides.title: Random K-fold flattered the same model by 0.02 AUC
slides.text: Lab 1.1, the course run Random K-fold flattered the same model by 0.02 AUC Random 5-fold 0.799 Grouped 5-fold 0.779 Held-out customers 0.785 Same configuration, same 5,000 orders. The held-out set is 14,289 orders of customers the model never saw.

slides.title: Average the top three configurations to make the baseline stable, not lucky
slides.text: The last step of the baseline Average the top three configurations to make the baseline stable, not lucky Why The single best of 20 is partly the best by chance. Three good ones disagree in different places. How Refit each on all training orders; average the probabilities. 0.784 held-out AUC of the three-model average; the single best scored 0.785 Here the average did not raise the score. It is kept because the catalog asks for a tuned, ensembled baseline: a pretrained model must beat the strongest version.

slides.title: Which estimate goes in the memo?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which estimate goes in the memo? Sarab's baseline scores 0.80 AUC under random 5-fold and 0.78 under 5-fold grouped by customer. Bustan will use the model on next quarter's orders, many from new customers. Which number goes in the memo? 0.80, because it is the model's best result 0.78, because the folds keep each customer on one side 0.79, the average of the two schemes Either, as long as the memo names the scheme

slides.title: A tuned baseline under a budget
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min A tuned baseline under a budget Tune a boosted-tree baseline under a fixed budget with grouped cross-validation: twenty random configurations on 5,000 orders, grouped by customer, against random K-fold, then a three-model ensemble (AI-off). D1_1_tune_boosted_tree.ipynb Load the orders and fix the budget 3 min Grouped folds by customer 5 min Random search under the budget 8 min Grouped against random K-fold 5 min Ensemble the top three 4 min ✱ Stretch: Spend the same budget on a finer grid of two parameters

slides.title: In-context learning on tables
slides.text: Session 2 In-context learning on tables Describe what a tabular foundation model learns in pretraining and what it does at prediction Run a pretrained tabular model on the same folds as the baseline Compare accuracy and run time with the tuning time included 02

slides.title: It reads your training rows as context and predicts in one pass, with no training on them
slides.text: What a tabular foundation model does It reads your training rows as context and predicts in one pass, with no training on them Pretraining once, by the vendor, on synthetic tables → Context your labelled training rows → Query your test rows → Output probabilities, one forward pass No parameter updates. "Fit" stores the rows; the work happens at prediction.

slides.title: The cost moves from fitting to predicting
slides.text: Where the seconds go The cost moves from fitting to predicting Boosted trees In-context model Fit builds trees stores rows Tuning many fits usually none Predict walks trees: cheap attends to training rows: grows with both sizes Hardware CPU GPU for large tables For Bustan Scoring 2,000 orders every night is cheap either way. Scoring 50,000 with 50,000 rows of context is not.

slides.title: Two families of tabular foundation models, with different licences
slides.text: The models in the tool slot Two families of tabular foundation models, with different licences TabICL (TabICLv2) Classification and regression. Code and weights under BSD-3-Clause, a permissive licence. TabPFN family (TabPFN-2.5, 2.6) Weights under Prior Labs' non-commercial licences: testing and research, not production, without a commercial licence. Names and licences change. Checked on the official pages in November 2026. Check again before a cohort.

slides.title: Score both models on the same folds and pair the differences
slides.text: The rule of Lab 1.2 Score both models on the same folds and pair the differences folds = U.grouped_folds(data.customer, 5) gbm = fold_scores(lambda: U.lgbm(**best_cfg), X, y, folds) pre = fold_scores(make_pretrained, X, y, folds) diff = pre.auc - gbm.auc # fold by fold U.mean_ci(diff) Paired A hard fold is hard for both models; the difference cancels it. Unpaired Each model on its own split adds split noise to the comparison.

slides.title: At 2,000 orders the two cannot be told apart, and one of them needed 40 seconds of tuning
slides.text: Lab 1.2, the course run (stand-in) At 2,000 orders the two cannot be told apart, and one of them needed 40 seconds of tuning Answered by AUC (5 folds) Fit s Predict s Tuning s Tuned LightGBM 0.779 ± 0.027 0.39 0.008 40 Stand-in 0.771 ± 0.035 0.23 0.073 0 Paired difference, stand-in minus baseline: -0.008, 95% interval -0.022 to +0.006.

slides.title: A pretrained model brings its own preprocessing: know what it does to your columns
slides.text: What changed besides the model A pretrained model brings its own preprocessing: know what it does to your columns Scaling Rescaled inside the model. Trees never needed it. Categories The segment is stored as a code 0 to 3. A careless pipeline feeds it as a number. Ensembling Several passes over transformed copies of the table (TabICL's n_estimators). Fairness cuts both ways. The pretrained model ensembles by default; that is why the baseline is ensembled too.

slides.title: What makes the run-time comparison fair?
slides.text: Checkpoint What makes the run-time comparison fair? The pretrained model took 0.3 seconds per fold and the baseline 0.4. Rafif concludes the pretrained model is cheaper. What is missing from his comparison? The type of processor each model ran on Nothing: fit time is the cost that matters The 103 fits the baseline's tuning cost before that fit The AUC of each model on the same folds

slides.title: A pretrained model on the same folds
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min A pretrained model on the same folds Run a pretrained tabular model on the same splits; compare accuracy and run time: the same grouped folds of 2,000 orders, the model's own preprocessing, and a table that counts the baseline's tuning time. D1_2_run_pretrained_tabular.ipynb Who answers: the model or the stand-in 3 min Same folds, same metric 6 min Fit and predict, timed 7 min The comparison table with tuning time 6 min What changed in the preprocessing 3 min ✱ Stretch: Give the pretrained model the raw categories and compare

slides.title: Learning curves decide
slides.text: Session 3 Learning curves decide Build learning curves from repeated subsamples at six training sizes Put an interval on each point and read where the curves cross State where each approach wins and where the evidence is too thin to say 03

slides.title: A score at one training size is one point on a curve
slides.text: Why one comparison is not enough A score at one training size is one point on a curve Bustan has 500 orders for a new segment and 50,000 for its oldest depots. Pretrained models are often strongest on small tables; tuned trees catch up as rows grow. Where the curves cross, if they cross, is the decision. Six sizes 500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000 orders in the lab; 50,000 supplied.

slides.title: Repeat every point on a fresh subsample to see how far it moves
slides.text: The design of Lab 1.3 Repeat every point on a fresh subsample to see how far it moves Draw n orders from the pool → Tune the baseline: 8 configurations, grouped folds → Score both on the same held-out customers → Repeat with a new seed The interval is over samples. It answers "what if Bustan had drawn other orders of this size?"

slides.title: On Bustan's late deliveries the two curves overlap at every size
slides.text: Lab 1.3, the course run (stand-in) On Bustan's late deliveries the two curves overlap at every size Training orders Tuned LightGBM, AUC (95% interval) Stand-in, AUC (95% interval) 500 0.740 (0.704 to 0.775) 0.750 (0.725 to 0.775) 2,000 0.768 (0.733 to 0.804) 0.765 (0.754 to 0.775) 10,000 0.777 (0.747 to 0.807) 0.774 (0.770 to 0.778) 50,000 (supplied) 0.775 (0.764 to 0.786) 0.777 (0.777 to 0.778) The paired difference at every size has an interval that contains zero: no size where one approach wins.

slides.title: A crossover counts only where the interval of the difference leaves zero
slides.text: How to read a learning curve A crossover counts only where the interval of the difference leaves zero Pretrained wins The whole interval of (pretrained minus baseline) above zero. Baseline wins The whole interval below zero. Cannot tell The interval contains zero. Say so, and say what more evidence would decide it. Overlapping error bars are not the test. Two bars can overlap while the paired difference is clear, because the repeats are paired.

slides.title: Do not extend a curve past its last measured size
slides.text: What the curve does not say Do not extend a curve past its last measured size The supplied 50,000-order point exists because the curve could not be guessed from 10,000. Run time grows differently: in the course run, 24 seconds for the baseline at 50,000 (tuning included) and 21 for the stand-in. A real in-context model at 50,000 rows needs a GPU; that is a cost line, not a footnote.

slides.title: What does this point say?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does this point say? At 500 orders, three repeats give the pretrained model a mean AUC 0.011 above the tuned baseline. The 95% interval of the paired difference runs from -0.031 to +0.052. What goes in the memo? No difference detectable at 500 orders with three repeats The pretrained model wins on small data The two models are equally accurate at 500 orders The comparison is invalid and should be dropped

slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Learning curves with intervals Plot both models across six training sizes, using supplied scores for the largest: repeated subsamples at 500 to 10,000 orders, intervals per point, and the supplied 50,000-order scores. D1_3_plot_both_across.ipynb The sizes and the repeats 4 min Score both models at each size 9 min Intervals per point 5 min Add the supplied largest size and plot 4 min Where each approach wins 3 min ✱ Stretch: Add the run time per size as a second panel

slides.title: Reading a leaderboard claim
slides.text: Session 4 Reading a leaderboard claim Find unequal tuning budgets in a benchmark table Remove datasets the pretrained model may have seen or been selected on Recount wins as a paired difference with an interval 04

slides.title: "Beats gradient boosting on 35 of 36 benchmark datasets"
slides.text: Rafif's email "Beats gradient boosting on 35 of 36 benchmark datasets" RafifLook at this slide from the vendor. 35 out of 36! Should we just switch? SarabSend me the table behind it, not the slide. Three questions for any claim Was the baseline tuned as much? Was the model scored on data it was built or selected on? How big is each win, with an interval?

slides.title: The claim's boosted trees got zero tuning trials; the pretrained model ensembled eight passes
slides.text: The first column to read The claim's boosted trees got zero tuning trials; the pretrained model ensembled eight passes 35 / 36 wins as claimed: defaults against an ensemble 23 / 36 wins against trees tuned with 100 trials 11 / 23 wins once overlapping datasets are removed

slides.title: A model scored on datasets it was selected on is grading its own homework
slides.text: The second column to read A model scored on datasets it was selected on is grading its own homework Pretraining overlap : the dataset, or a copy, was in the training data. Selection overlap : the dataset was used to choose the model's settings or checkpoint. Either inflates the score on exactly that dataset. In the table 13 of 36 datasets carry the flag. Drop them before counting. Pretraining on synthetic tables lowers the risk of the first kind; public validation suites keep the second alive.

slides.title: Without overlap the average advantage is zero; it splits by table size
slides.text: The third question Without overlap the average advantage is zero; it splits by table size Clean datasets Count Pretrained minus tuned, AUC 95% interval All 23 -0.0005 -0.005 to +0.004 Under 3,000 rows 10 +0.009 +0.005 to +0.013 3,000 rows or more 13 -0.008 -0.011 to -0.005 A bootstrap over datasets. Counting wins hid both effects.

slides.title: Someone else's benchmark sets a hypothesis; your own curve tests it
slides.text: The reply Someone else's benchmark sets a hypothesis; your own curve tests it The claim compared an eight-member pretrained ensemble with untuned trees. At equal tuning and without the 13 overlapping datasets, the advantage is zero on average: positive under 3,000 rows, negative above. On our late-delivery data the two approaches cannot be told apart at any size from 500 to 50,000 orders.

slides.title: Which fact voids the claim first?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which fact voids the claim first? A benchmark table shows a pretrained model winning 30 of 32 datasets. Which single fact, if true, most undermines the claim? The pretrained model was slower on every dataset Most of the datasets are publicly available Half of the datasets have fewer than 3,000 rows The boosted trees were run at default settings

slides.title: Check a leaderboard claim
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min Check a leaderboard claim Check a claim for unequal tuning budgets and pretraining overlap: recount a vendor benchmark table at equal budgets, drop overlapping datasets and put an interval on the paired difference. D1_4_check_claim_unequal.ipynb Read the claim and its table 4 min Equal budgets 6 min Drop overlap 5 min Paired difference with an interval 6 min Set it beside your own curve 4 min ✱ Stretch: Count how many datasets the claim would need to hold at equal budget

slides.title: A fair comparison is designed before it is run
slides.text: Day 1 · Three things to keep A fair comparison is designed before it is run Budget and folds Write the tuning budget down; keep each customer on one side. Curves, not points Compare across sizes, with intervals of the paired difference. Claims are hypotheses Equal budgets, no overlap, an interval; then your own data.

slides.title: Forecasting with pretrained models
slides.text: Today Forecasting with pretrained models Session 1 · Zero-shot against a benchmark floor A zero-shot forecaster is one more method in the same rolling-origin backtest, scored on the same windows Session 2 · Where zero-shot loses An average over 400 series hides the groups where a benchmark wins Session 3 · Holidays that move Ramadan comes about eleven days earlier each Gregorian year, so a yearly lag misses it and a covariate finds it Session 4 · Ensembles worth their cost A stack learned on earlier windows must beat the best single model on later windows by more than its interval

slides.title: What would change Sarab's verdict?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 What would change Sarab's verdict? Yesterday the learning curves of the tuned baseline and the pretrained model overlapped at every size, with paired intervals around zero. Which new evidence would justify writing "the pretrained model wins below 1,000 orders"? A vendor table with 35 wins out of 36 A higher mean AUC at 500 orders in one more run More repeats at 500 and 1,000 orders whose paired interval stays above zero Rerunning the curves with random K-fold instead of held-out customers

slides.title: A forecaster counts only if it beats the floor in a rolling-origin backtest
slides.text: Recap from DS-304, not retaught A forecaster counts only if it beats the floor in a rolling-origin backtest Origin cut the history at a date → Forecast 28 days ahead from what was known → Score against what happened → Roll to the next origin DS-304 built the floor, the smoothing and ARIMA models, Hijri regressors and the simple average. Today they are supplied: six origins, 400 series, three benchmarks.

slides.title: Zero-shot against a benchmark floor
slides.text: Session 1 Zero-shot against a benchmark floor Run a zero-shot forecaster on 400 series at four origins Score scaled point error and quantile loss on the same windows as supplied benchmarks Report each method against the seasonal naive floor 01

slides.title: A zero-shot forecaster needs no training on your series, but it is scored like any other method
slides.text: What changes with a pretrained forecaster A zero-shot forecaster needs no training on your series, but it is scored like any other method Input : each series' history up to the origin. No product, no depot, no features unless you pass covariates. Output : quantiles for the next 28 days. No fit on Bustan's data, so no tuning budget, and nothing to retrain each month. Same windows as the benchmarks, or the comparison means nothing. Chronos-2 A pretrained model for univariate, multivariate and covariate-informed forecasting, trained on synthetic data. Weights under Apache-2.0.

slides.title: Divide every error by the series' own scale, or the staples decide alone
slides.text: Two numbers per series and origin Divide every error by the series' own scale, or the staples decide alone Score What it measures Read MASE mean absolute error of the median, divided by the in-sample error of last week's copy below 1 beats the naive in-sample Scaled quantile loss pinball loss over the 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 quantiles, same scale rewards sharp bands that still hold 80% coverage share of days inside the 0.1 to 0.9 band should be near 80%

slides.title: The pinball loss charges a quantile forecast unequally for being low and being high
slides.text: The loss behind every quantile The pinball loss charges a quantile forecast unequally for being low and being high def pinball(y, q, tau): d = y - q return np.maximum(tau * d, (tau - 1) * d) # tau = 0.9: a forecast 10 below costs 9, # a forecast 10 above costs 1 Tomorrow's decision The same asymmetry is the newsvendor's: when a shortage costs nine times a leftover, order the 0.9 quantile. Day 3 starts here.

slides.title: The zero-shot forecaster beats the floor and smoothing, not the tuned LightGBM
slides.text: Lab 2.1, the course run (stand-in), four origins, 1,504 series-origins The zero-shot forecaster beats the floor and smoothing, not the tuned LightGBM Method MASE Scaled quantile loss Loss against the floor 80% coverage Seasonal naive (floor) 1.141 0.811 1.000 75% Smoothing 0.973 0.676 0.833 71% Zero-shot (stand-in) 0.883 0.610 0.751 74% LightGBM, tuned 0.722 0.491 0.605 81%

slides.title: Same origins, same horizon, same series, same scale
slides.text: What makes the comparison fair Same origins, same horizon, same series, same scale Fair The zero-shot model is run at the four origins of the supplied backtests and scored with the same function. Unfair A vendor's accuracy on its benchmark, set beside Bustan's backtest. Different series, different windows, different scale. Check it in code. Lab 2.1 asserts that your scores match the helper's before printing a table.

slides.title: Is the zero-shot forecaster useful here?
slides.text: Checkpoint Is the zero-shot forecaster useful here? The zero-shot forecaster scores 0.75 of the floor's quantile loss; the tuned LightGBM scores 0.61. Ahlam asks whether the pretrained model is worth keeping. What is the best answer today? Not as a replacement; test where it wins and what it adds to an ensemble first No: it loses to LightGBM, so it has no use Yes: it needs no training, so it should replace LightGBM Yes: it beats the floor, which is all a forecaster must do

slides.title: Where zero-shot loses
slides.text: Session 2 Where zero-shot loses Classify series as smooth, intermittent or short from their own history Compare methods by series group, point and quantile Turn a group table into a routing rule 02

slides.title: An average over 400 series hides the groups where a method fails
slides.text: Why one number is not enough An average over 400 series hides the groups where a method fails Regular 160 series: staples and dairy, sold most days. Intermittent 100 series: specialty imports and catering items, many zero days. Ramadan items 80 series: dates and juices, from the product master. Short 60 series: products launched in the last six months.

slides.title: Two numbers describe a demand pattern: how often it sells, and how much the sizes vary
slides.text: Classifying from the series itself Two numbers describe a demand pattern: how often it sells, and how much the sizes vary ADI : average days between non-zero days over the last year. CV squared : variability of the non-zero sizes. In the lab: short under 180 days of history; intermittent when ADI is 1.32 or more; the rest regular. A class has a date A product launched in December is short in October and regular by May. Classify at the origin you forecast from.

slides.title: The tuned LightGBM wins every group; the zero-shot gap is smallest on intermittent items
slides.text: Lab 2.2, the course run (stand-in), scaled quantile loss The tuned LightGBM wins every group; the zero-shot gap is smallest on intermittent items Group Seasonal naive Smoothing Zero-shot LightGBM Zero-shot gap Intermittent 0.792 0.662 0.501 0.469 +0.032 Regular 0.715 0.559 0.551 0.440 +0.112 Short 0.958 0.848 0.839 0.653 +0.186 Ramadan items 0.962 0.851 0.760 0.549 +0.211 The gap is the paired difference, zero-shot minus LightGBM; every interval excludes zero. Against smoothing, the zero-shot model ties on short series.

slides.title: A short series borrows strength from other series, or it has nothing to learn from
slides.text: Recap from DS-304, applied A short series borrows strength from other series, or it has nothing to learn from Global model The LightGBM learns from all 400 series at once, so a new product starts with its category's pattern. Zero-shot, one series Sees only the product's own few weeks; the stand-in falls back to its last eight weeks. In context, many series Models that read a group of related series together can borrow without training.

slides.title: Choose the method per group on earlier windows, then score it on later ones
slides.text: From a group table to a rule Choose the method per group on earlier windows, then score it on later ones Group Chosen on 2025-10-05 and 2025-11-16 Why Regular, intermittent, Ramadan items LightGBM, tuned lowest loss on the earlier windows Short zero-shot no short series existed then: a method that needs no history A rule picked on the scored windows scores itself. It will look better than it will be next quarter.

slides.title: What do you do with this group?
slides.text: Checkpoint What do you do with this group? For 60 short series the zero-shot forecaster and smoothing differ by -0.009 in scaled quantile loss, with a 95% interval from -0.064 to +0.050. Both trail LightGBM by about 0.19. What do you recommend for new products? Switch new products to the zero-shot model, which scored lower Keep smoothing because the two are proven equal Treat short series as unforecastable and order by hand Use the tuned LightGBM, which wins the group, and retest the pretrained model later

slides.title: Holidays that move
slides.text: Session 3 Holidays that move Show why a yearly lag must respect both the week and the Hijri year Supply Ramadan and Eid as known future covariates Measure error in holiday weeks separately from ordinary weeks 03

slides.title: Demand follows the week and the Hijri year at once, and they do not line up
slides.text: Why holidays break yearly lags Demand follows the week and the Hijri year at once, and they do not line up 364 days 52 weeks: same weekday, but Ramadan has moved about eleven days. 354 days One Hijri year: right Ramadan day, wrong weekday. 357 days 51 weeks: same weekday, within three days of the Hijri date. Ramadan 1446 began on 1 March 2025; Ramadan 1447 on 18 February 2026 (Umm al-Qura).

slides.title: From pre-Ramadan to Eid al-Fitr, the 51-week lag beats both yearly lags
slides.text: Lab 2.3, the course run From pre-Ramadan to Eid al-Fitr, the 51-week lag beats both yearly lags Lag 354 days 0.615 Lag 364 days 0.574 Lag 357 days 0.487 Mean absolute error relative to the window's mean, 80 Ramadan items, 4 February to 23 March 2026.

slides.title: The calendar is a known future covariate; next week's sales are not
slides.text: What may go into a forecast The calendar is a known future covariate; next week's sales are not Input Known at the origin? slides.title: The simple average is hard to beat; learned weights must earn their extra risk
slides.text: Recap from DS-304, then one step further The simple average is hard to beat; learned weights must earn their extra risk Simple average No weights to estimate, so nothing to overfit. Works when the members are comparably good. Stacking Weights learned from earlier forecasts. Wins when the members differ in quality, if the weights are estimated honestly.

Each was made without its own answers.

slides.title: Asymmetric costs
slides.text: Session 1 Asymmetric costs Compute underage and overage costs from a cost table Turn a critical ratio into an order quantity from quantile forecasts Measure the cost of ordering the median instead 01

slides.title: A case short and a case left over do not cost the same
slides.text: What a wrong order costs A case short and a case left over do not cost the same Underage: one case short The lost margin, price minus cost, plus goodwill worth half the margin: the customer may order elsewhere next week. Overage: one case left over Holding at 0.4% of the cost per day for a week; for products that keep 30 days or less, 60% of the cost lost to spoilage. Bustan's cost table is synthetic: the rates are the course's, set to look like a food wholesaler's, not quoted from one.

slides.title: Order up to the demand quantile at underage / (underage + overage)
slides.text: The newsvendor result Order up to the demand quantile at underage / (underage + overage) Costs underage, overage per case → Critical ratio u / (u + o) → Quantile of the week's demand → Order rounded up to cases Takeaway. The mean is the right order only when a shortage and a leftover cost the same.

slides.title: Same forecaster, opposite decisions: dry goods above the median, dairy below it
slides.text: Lab 3.1, the course run, 20 products at the Riyadh depot Same forecaster, opposite decisions: dry goods above the median, dairy below it Category Critical ratio Order Rice, flour, sugar 0.82 to 0.92 well above the median Beverages 0.83 to 0.92 well above the median Dates 0.83 to 0.91 well above the median Chilled dairy (21 days) 0.17 to 0.33 below the median

slides.title: Add the daily medians; add the daily variances, not the spreads
slides.text: The forecaster gives days; Imad orders weeks Add the daily medians; add the daily variances, not the spreads mu = q[:, 1].sum(axis=1) # sum of daily medians sd = np.sqrt((((q[:, 2] - q[:, 0]) / 2.563) ** 2).sum(axis=1)) # 0.1 to 0.9 spans 2.563 sd order = np.ceil(np.maximum(mu + sd * stats.norm.ppf(cr), 0)) Two assumptions. Days are independent and the bands are right. Session 4 tests both on Bustan's own errors.

slides.title: The 20 orders share trucks, two reefers and 200 cubic metres of depot space
slides.text: Why one rule per product is not enough The 20 orders share trucks, two reefers and 200 cubic metres of depot space Trucks 60 m3 and 20 tonnes, SAR 2,400 a trip, one supplier per truck. Reefers Dairy only: 40 m3 and 14 tonnes, SAR 3,200 a trip, two a week. Depot space 200 m3 received a week at Riyadh. The newsvendor orders need 218.8.

slides.title: Variables, an objective and constraints, solved together by HiGHS
slides.text: From rule to programme Variables, an objective and constraints, solved together by HiGHS q[i] = prob.add_variable(f"q_{p}", lowBound=0, cat="Integer") # cases trucks[s] = prob.add_variable(f"trucks_{s}", lowBound=0, cat="Integer") prob += trip_cost * trucks + underage * short + overage * over # objective prob += q[i] - target[i] == over[i] - short[i] # distance from target prob += lpSum(case_m3 * q[i] for i in s) <= 60 * trucks[s], f"m3_{s}" # and kg_, reefers prob += lpSum(case_m3 * q[i]) <= 200, "depot_space" prob.solve(pulp.HiGHS(msg=False))

slides.title: Half a truck costs a whole trip, so trucks are integer variables
slides.text: Why whole numbers matter Half a truck costs a whole trip, so trucks are integer variables Continuous 1.26 trucks of dry goods at SAR 3,014: a price no driver charges. The plan looks cheaper than it is. Integer One truck or two. The solver searches the whole numbers (branch and bound) and proves the best.

Inbound 200.0 of 200 m3. Ten more cubic metres would save SAR 1,703 that week.

slides.title: A constraint binds when it has no slack; it matters when relaxing it lowers the cost
slides.text: Reading the solution A constraint binds when it has no slack; it matters when relaxing it lowers the cost Constraint Slack Relax it by one unit depot_space 0.02 m3 10 m3 saves SAR 1,703 reefers 0 reefers a third reefer saves nothing: the two have 26.5 m3 free kg_S1 1 kg tight because the cut was sized to fit one truck

slides.title: Should Imad pay for a third reefer?
slides.text: Checkpoint Should Imad pay for a third reefer? The plan uses both reefers, so the reefer constraint has zero slack. The two reefers carry 53.5 of their 80 cubic metres. A haulier offers a third reefer for SAR 900 this week. What do you tell Imad? Accept: the reefer constraint binds, so more reefers help Decline: re-solving with three reefers would not change the plan, because dairy already fits Accept: a third reefer frees depot space for dry goods Accept: it is cheaper than the SAR 1,703 that capacity is worth

slides.title: Scoring by regret
slides.text: Session 3 Scoring by regret Compute the realised cost of a plan made from each forecaster Compute regret against the plan made with hindsight Compare the ranking by regret with the ranking by error 03

slides.title: Regret is what the order cost, minus what the best order in hindsight would have cost
slides.text: Scoring a forecaster by its decisions Regret is what the order cost, minus what the best order in hindsight would have cost Forecast quantiles for the week → Order the critical quantile → Demand happens cost of short and left over → Regret minus the hindsight cost Takeaway. Without capacity limits the hindsight order is the demand itself, so regret is the realised cost.

slides.title: Error weighs every quantile and product alike; regret weighs them by what they cost
slides.text: Why the two scores can disagree Error weighs every quantile and product alike; regret weighs them by what they cost Scaled quantile loss The 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9 quantiles of every product, each scaled to its own series. Regret The 0.9 quantile of rice and the 0.25 quantile of dairy, in riyals: a dairy leftover costs SAR 40 to 97 a case.

The scaled quantile loss was computed wrongly Regret depends on demand, not on the forecaster Its errors fell where they cost most: dairy overage and the Eid al-Adha week Smoothing is the better forecaster for Bustan

slides.title: A plan that is right on average can still run short in the weeks that matter
slides.text: What the expected cost hides A plan that is right on average can still run short in the weeks that matter Simulate 2,000 weeks of demand from the forecast and run the fixed plan through them. Report per product: the share of weeks with a shortage and the fill rate. Check the assumptions on past errors: are the bands the right width, are days and products independent?

slides.title: One shock shared by all products, one per product-week, one per day
slides.text: Building correlated scenarios One shock shared by all products, one per product-week, one per day a = np.sqrt(rho_prod) # all products, same week b = np.sqrt(max(rho_day - rho_prod, 0)) # one product, all its days c = np.sqrt(1 - a**2 - b**2) # the rest, day by day z = a * N(n, 1, 1) + b * N(n, 20, 1) + c * N(n, 20, 7) daily = np.maximum(mu + scale * sd * z, 0)

slides.text: Checkpoint How likely are two shortages together? Rice and sugar each run short in 10% of weeks. A planner reports a 1% chance that both run short in the same week. When a shared shock, such as a pre-Eid rush, lifts both demands in the same week When both come from the same supplier When each product's days are independent of each other When the forecaster's bands are too wide

slides.title: Correcting for shift
slides.text: Session 3 Correcting for shift Recall split conformal intervals and the exchangeability they assume Estimate density-ratio weights from an adversarial classifier Apply weighted conformal intervals and check coverage in the new region 03

slides.title: Split conformal holds 90% of the time only if new orders are exchangeable with the calibration orders
slides.text: Recap from DS-305, then what breaks Split conformal holds 90% of the time only if new orders are exchangeable with the calibration orders scores = np.abs(y_cal - model.predict(X_cal)) # log hours k = int(np.ceil((n + 1) * 0.9)) q = np.sort(scores)[k - 1] # interval: prediction ± q Lab 4.1's adversarial AUC of 0.95 says the northern orders are not exchangeable with the old ones.

slides.title: Weight each calibration order by how northern it looks
slides.text: Correcting for covariate shift Weight each calibration order by how northern it looks Classifier p(north | x), out of fold → Ratio w(x) = p / (1 - p) → Weighted quantile of calibration scores, plus the new order's own weight at infinity Takeaway. If too few calibration orders look like a new one, its interval is infinite: an honest "we do not know".

slides.title: Weighting restores 90% overall, and leaves institutional customers short
slides.text: Lab 4.3, the course run, 90% intervals for delivery hours in the north Weighting restores 90% overall, and leaves institutional customers short Northern orders Split conformal Weighted All 87.7% 90.1% Grocery 89.0% 91.4% HoReCa 85.5% 88.2% Hypermarket 95.2% 96.5% Institutional 78.7% 81.0% Median width 61 hours split, 67 weighted. Effective sample size 1,082 of 22,325 calibration orders.

slides.title: What did the weights correct?
slides.text: Checkpoint What did the weights correct? After weighting, coverage in the north is 90.1% overall but 81.0% for institutional customers. Which statement is right? The weights are wrong: weighted conformal guarantees 90% in every segment Institutional customers are too few to measure coverage Raising the institutional weights would fix it Weights correct a change in the inputs; the institutional gap is a change in the link, which needs northern outcomes

The task reads Bustan's orders with customer ids. What blocks it first? The price per prediction The licence: its outputs are for non-commercial use only The benchmark score is not high enough Only the transfer of personal data outside the Kingdom

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How presentations are scored The rubric Fair comparison 25% Validation under shift 25% Ensemble or decision analysis 20% Adoption reasoning 15% Reproducibility 15% Show results from at least two measured runs. A claim without a number is a plan, not a result.

slides.title: Ten minutes to defend the decision, ten minutes of questions from two assessors
slides.text: Format Ten minutes to defend the decision, ten minutes of questions from two assessors 1 · The task and the decision Which task, who decides, what is decided. One slide. 2 · The protocol The tuned baseline and its budget, two pretrained candidates, the ensemble, the validation scheme and the shift it matches. 3 · Results and conditions Every number with its interval and its run; regret where a decision follows; the adoption decision with its conditions. Peer feedback. After each defence, everyone writes one strength, one question and one suggestion.

slides.title: An assessor names a new shift; you predict which result changes before you re-run
slides.text: Inside the ten minutes of questions An assessor names a new shift; you predict which result changes before you re-run Scenario e.g. a third region, a supplier change, Ramadan inside the test window → Prediction which validation number moves, and which way → Re-run the protocol on the new split, live or right after What earns the marks. A prediction with a reason, then an honest comparison with the re-run, whichever way it went.
